title: Psychedelics and the essential importance of context

claims.statement: In adults who planned, on their own initiative, to take a classic psychedelic, a better state of mind measured before the drug is associated with a less challenging experience, and in laboratory LSD sessions mood and personality measured before the dose were associated with how the session went; many of the larger associations reported come from people recalling afterwards how they had felt. In the only prospective study outside a laboratory among these sources (Haijen et al., 2018; self-selected adults who answered online surveys; of the 379 who reported back, 48% took LSD or 1P-LSD, 29% psilocybin and 11% ayahuasca), feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious and in a good mood, rated by the participants within the day before ('set'), went with lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores they gave about a day after (standardized beta −0.32, SE 0.07; moderate in the editors' terms), as did recreational or social intentions rated a week before (−0.22; small). Strong expectations and a clear intention went with higher mystical-type (0.18) and visual (0.16) scores but not clearly with challenge, and set was unrelated to mystical-type scores. The trait absorption went with more intense experiences of every kind, challenging (0.22) as well as mystical-type (0.35), while trait anxiety, openness, emotional stability, suggestibility and the number of earlier psychedelic experiences showed no statistically significant association with any of them in this model of about 198 people. The sample shrank from 654 a week before to about 198 in this analysis (editors' inference), and the predictors were adjusted for one another and for an amount the participants estimated after the experience, not for the drug taken or psychiatric history. Average well-being rose from 49.0 before to 52.6 two weeks after, with no comparison group and fewer than half the sample remaining, and mystical-type scores no longer predicted it once traits, intentions, set and setting were in the model. In healthy volunteers given LSD, mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room and mostly with a placebo session for comparison (nine Basel laboratory studies, 213 people; Vizeli et al., 2024), higher well-being rated on a mood questionnaire before the dose went with stronger effects on every self-rated scale except a rating of a bad drug effect and two others, the anxiety scales included, so in these sessions a better mood went with a stronger experience rather than a less challenging one; anxiety rated before the dose went with more anxiety during the session, and openness with more mystical-type ratings, all at a given dose; the text gives no sizes. In two retrospective studies of people who had used psilocybin, as summarized by a systematic review the editors rate critically low (Aday et al., 2021), states recalled after the experience were associated with it; in the one for which the review gives figures (143 people), surrender correlated with mystical-type experience (r = 0.72) and preoccupation and confusion with dread (0.64 and 0.58). In a US online panel, people who blamed a negative mindset for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.14) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others afterwards (odds ratio 4.56, 95% CI 2.10 to 9.94, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any; Simonsson et al., 2023). Such recalled states are associations reported by the same people at the same sitting, not predictors. An opinion piece by the same research group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, in one figure and without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same online survey (266 people who completed four surveys): readiness, a clear intention with strong expectations, and trust in the people who would be present, all rated before the experience, went with less challenging experiences; because it gives no measures, sample description or model details and its sample overlaps the prospective study's, it is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. Preparation is routine in clinical trials, but none of those reviewed compared different kinds of it: a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; it mapped what the trials reported, without appraising them or combining their outcomes), found that 21 described giving information about the effects, 19 meetings beforehand to build trust (mostly one to four, of about 2 hours each) and 18 advice on the attitude to take, mostly openness and letting go, and that no included trial compared different preparation, sets or settings; the review's remark that one trial's two-interview preparation made the experience and its benefits greater rests on a trial that did not vary preparation. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018), standardized coefficients adjusted for one another and for self-estimated amount (about 198 people): set and challenging experience −0.32 (SE 0.07); recreational or social intentions −0.22 (SE 0.08); clear intentions and mystical-type 0.18, visual 0.16, challenging −0.13 (p = 0.088); absorption and challenging 0.22, mystical-type 0.35; R2 0.32 for challenging experience. Vizeli et al. (2024): directions and significance only (sizes are in a figure and a supplement not used): pre-dose well-being with stronger effects on all self-rated scales but three, the anxiety scales included; pre-dose anxiety with more anxiety during the session. Recalled afterwards: surrender r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation 0.64 and confusion 0.58 with dread (n = 143, one of the two retrospective studies, as summarized by Aday et al., 2021); negative mindset blamed for the most challenging experience: beta 0.14, harm thoughts or attempts OR 4.56 (95% CI 2.10 to 9.94), adjusted only for the other attributions (Simonsson et al., 2023).

claims.statement: In people who use classic psychedelics, feeling safe and supported is associated with fewer reported difficulties in retrospective surveys, while the only prospective study among these sources found only a weak, uncertain link for the place and the people. In that study (Haijen et al., 2018; about 198 self-selected adults who planned an experience on their own initiative), a good feeling about the people who would be present and about the place, rated within the day before, went with slightly lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores rated about a day after (standardized beta −0.14, p = 0.070, not statistically significant), and with slightly higher well-being two weeks later (1.2 points on the well-being scale per standard deviation of the rating, p = 0.037, one of many coefficients in a model without correction for multiple tests; not significant at four weeks, p = 0.077); a retreat or a setting designed for therapy, reported afterwards in two yes-or-no questions that the authors combined into one variable, showed no statistically significant association with any acute measure (0.02), and the authors note that the term was not defined for participants. In an international online survey of 6,877 self-selected people who had drunk ayahuasca, each point higher on a 1-to-4 rating of support and safety at their last ceremony went with 0.29 points less extreme fear or panic on a 0-to-10 scale (95% CI 0.15 to 0.43, editors' calculation), slightly fewer difficulties in the weeks after, and current distress lower by 0.62 points on the 40-point Kessler scale, under 2 points across the whole rating (editors' arithmetic), after adjustment for age, sex, education, mental-health diagnoses, times drunk and years since the last drink and for the motivation, ceremony and other support variables; the ratings were made looking back by the same people, and averaged near the top of the scale (Perkins et al., 2021). Among 613 US adults in an online panel who had used a classic psychedelic, those who blamed a lack of psychological support for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.25) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the days or weeks after (odds ratio 2.85, 95% CI 1.27 to 6.42, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any); blaming a disagreeable physical environment went with a smaller difference in challenge (0.09) and no detectable difference in harm thoughts, and blaming the people around with no statistically significant difference in either (odds ratio for harm thoughts 0.33, 0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051, lower if anything) (Simonsson et al., 2023). Among 163 experienced people recalling two experiences, mostly at home or at a friend's house, those whose experience was at a party, club or festival (24 first and 12 most recent experiences) had higher average challenge scores than the rest (19 against 17 and 31 against 16 per cent of the maximum), a comparison the authors did not test (Palmer and Maynard, 2022). An opinion piece by the same group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same survey (266 people who completed four surveys), in which a 'therapeutic setting' (how it was recorded is not given) went with more peak or mystical-type experiences and trust in the people who would be present, rated beforehand, with less challenging ones; in the prospective study above, which appears to be the fuller report, a similar rating of the people and the place showed only a non-significant trend and a retreat or therapeutic setting no statistically significant association, so the preview is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. No study read here put people in different places or company on purpose to compare them. The same opinion piece states that, by 2018 and apart from a dose study, retrospective analyses and one 1969 study, controlled studies isolating contextual factors had not been done, and a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023, found no trial that compared settings (Estric et al., 2025; the trials were not appraised); in those trials, 12 kept two staff in the room throughout the session and five, published in 2023, one per participant, and rooms ranged from a hospital room left unchanged (4 trials) to one disguised as a living room or decorated, a choice the review's authors judged to have been made without evidence. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018): setting component and challenging experience beta −0.14 (p = 0.070); setting component and well-being at two weeks 1.2 points per standard deviation (p = 0.037; at four weeks p = 0.077); retreat or therapeutic setting 0.02 (p = 0.81). Perkins et al. (2021), per point of a 1-to-4 support-and-safety rating: extreme fear (0 to 10) −0.29 (95% CI −0.43 to −0.15, editors'), integration difficulties −0.13, Kessler-10 −0.62 (under 2 points across the whole rating); the paper does not say which outcomes were modelled as ordinal, so reading −0.29 as points on the fear item assumes a linear model. Simonsson et al. (2023), attributions of the most challenging experience, adjusted only for the other attributions: no support beta 0.25, harm thoughts or attempts OR 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42); disagreeable physical environment 0.09, OR 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35); disagreeable social environment not associated, OR 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01, p = 0.051). Palmer and Maynard (2022), untested: party settings 19.27 against 16.77 (first) and 31.46 against 16.16 (most recent) per cent of the maximum CEQ score.
